title: Phones under Rs 7,000 fell 94%: why AI made cheap phones vanish
subtitle: Plus the new PF withdrawal rules, a strong rupee and IT pay, a big drop in wheat sowing, and a 31-month high for core industries.
content_html:
Picture walking into a phone shop with Rs 7,000 in your pocket and finding almost nothing to buy. That is close to what happened in India this festive season. According to CyberMedia Research (CMR), reported by Business Standard on 20 November 2026, shipments of phones under Rs 7,000 fell 94% from July to September, compared with the same three months last year. And the reason is not in India at all. Here is that story, plus four more from the same day.

Where did the cheap phones go?

The short answer: AI. Big AI data centres around the world need huge amounts of memory chips. Data centres buy so many that these chips got costlier for phone makers too. Business Standard says makers had little room to swallow the extra cost, so they put a part of it into the price you pay.

Think of a samosa stall. If oil doubles in price, either the samosa costs more, or the cheapest one stops being made. Phones are going through the same thing.

Research firm IDC says in its report of 17 November 2026 that India shipped 36.8 million smartphones from July to September 2026. That is 23.3% fewer than a year ago, the steepest fall since late 2022, and the weakest festive quarter in a decade. CMR and Counterpoint Research put the fall at 20%.

Costly phones did fine

Not every phone suffered. CMR's numbers show a clear split by price:

  • Under Rs 7,000: down 94%
  • Rs 7,000 to Rs 24,999: down 42%
  • Rs 25,000 to Rs 49,000: up 38%
  • Rs 50,000 to Rs 1 lakh: up 32%

The average selling price (ASP) is the money made by selling phones, divided by the number of phones sold. IDC says India's ASP rose 26.1% in a year, to a record $371. Even so, the total value of the market fell 3.3%, because so many fewer phones were sold.

Smaller festive discounts, more EMI

Counterpoint looked at the festive days from 8 October to 10 November. Phone sales in that period fell 22% from last year, the same Business Standard report says. Festive discounts shrank to 10 to 25%, down from 35 to 40% in 2025. So brands leaned on no-cost EMI instead. EMI means paying for something in equal monthly parts, like paying a friend back Rs 1,000 a month instead of Rs 12,000 at once. Counterpoint says 48% of festive phone sales were bought with some kind of loan or EMI.

Also, Indian phone brands grew their share of the market from 2% to 7% in a year (Counterpoint). And in IDC's top 10 list, Samsung was the only brand that sold more phones than last year, up 7.9%.

New PF rules: your money, sooner

The second story is about PF, the provident fund. It is a savings pot that you and your employer fill every month. On 19 November 2026, the board that runs the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) approved some big changes, Business Standard reported:

  • Full PF after 2 months without work. If you leave your work and stay without work, you can take out your full PF after 2 months, not 12.
  • Up to 90% when you need it. The amount you must leave in the account drops from 25% to 10%. So members can now reach up to 90% of their PF for allowed needs like a house, medical care or education, up from 75%.
  • Monthly money at retirement. Retiring members can choose to take their PF in monthly, quarterly or half-yearly parts, while the rest keeps earning interest. This is optional.

The Labour Ministry says about 6.32 lakh EPF members above 55 years of age, with more than Rs 5 lakh in their PF, are expected to gain first from the monthly payout plan, YourStory reported. This plan is separate from the monthly EPS pension.

A stronger rupee, a smaller IT bonus?

Third, the rupee. Since the start of October, the rupee has gained 2.5% against the US dollar, 6.2% against the euro and 3.4% against the British pound, according to a report from the broker Kotak, covered by The Economic Times. On 18 November the rupee closed at about Rs 93.41 per dollar, its strongest level since April 2026, Upstox News reported.

That sounds like good news, so why do IT companies worry? They earn mostly in dollars, euros and pounds, but pay most of their bills in rupees. When the rupee gets stronger, each dollar they earn turns into fewer rupees. If an uncle abroad sends you $100 a month, a stronger rupee means less pocket money from the same $100.

Kotak estimates that this could lower IT companies' profit per share for the year to March 2027 by 4 to 13%, for companies that have not hedged. Hedging means locking in an exchange rate in advance, like booking a train ticket early so a price jump later does not hurt. The report says companies could soften the blow with lower variable pay, the part of a salary linked to performance, and by cutting other spending.

Wheat sowing may fall the most in 26 years

Fourth, the farm. India's wheat area is set for its steepest fall in 26 years, industry officials told Reuters, in a report carried by Business Standard. The June to September monsoon rains were the lowest in more than a decade, so many fields are short of water. Wheat needs a lot of water. So in many states, farmers are moving to crops like chana (chickpeas) and rapeseed, which need less water and now pay better.

Government data shows wheat was planted on 5 million hectares by 13 November, 15.3% less than a year earlier. The average estimate of 10 industry officials is that the full season's area will fall about 6%, to 31.58 million hectares. In Punjab and Haryana, which have good irrigation, wheat area is likely to stay largely steady.

The government raised the minimum support price (MSP) for wheat by just 1%, to Rs 2,610 for 100 kg. MSP is the price the government promises to pay farmers when it buys their crop. Reuters says less wheat could push up wheat prices, which means the atta in your kitchen could cost more.

Core industries grow fast, with a catch

Last, factories and power plants. The output of India's nine core industries, like coal, power, steel and cement, grew 10.9% in October 2026, the highest in over a year and the best since a new data series began, according to Ministry of Commerce and Industry data reported by Deccan Herald on 20 November. These nine make up about 40% of India's index of industrial output.

Electricity rose 21.6% and cement 15.4%. But there is a catch. Last October, growth was just 0.8%. That makes this year look bigger, because it is compared with a very weak month. Aditi Nayar, chief economist at ICRA, said that from April to October, growth without electricity was only about 3.2%.

Three lessons for small businesses

The reel ends with three tips from these stories:

  1. Offer EMI. Almost half of festive phone sales (48%) were bought with a loan or EMI, Counterpoint found.
  2. Earn abroad? Check the currency risk. A stronger rupee could lower IT profit by 4 to 13%, Kotak estimates.
  3. Plan for atta costs. If wheat prices rise, a bakery, a dhaba or a tiffin service will feel it first.
